# Introduction 

Package `gtfs2gps` allows users to convert public transport GTFS data 
into a single `data.table` format with GPS-like records, tracking the 
space-time position of individual vehicles at high spatial and temporal 
resolutions. This GPS-like data format is quite convinient as it can be
easily used in various applications for running transport simulations, 
scenario analyses, data visualizations etc. 

To start using the package, you can install it from CRAN:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("gtfs2gps")
```

# Loading data

After loading the package, you can read a GTFS feed using `read_gtfs()`.
This function gets a zipped GTFS file and returns a list of `data.table` 
objects. To demonstrate the package, we will use a small sample of the 
GTFS from Porto Alegre, Brazil

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library("gtfs2gps")

# path to gtfs file
gtfs_file <- system.file("extdata/poa.zip", package ="gtfs2gps")

# read gtfs to memory 
poa <- gtfs2gps::read_gtfs(gtfs_file)

names(poa)
```

The returning list contains the tables from the GTFS file indexed 
according to their file names. Note that this function only loads 
those tables that are necessary for the operations in {gtfs2gps},
which are:
- `shapes.txt`
- `stop_times.txt`
- `stops.txt`
- `trips.txt`
- `agency.txt` (optional)
- `calendar.txt` (optional)
- `routes.txt` (optional)
- `frequencies.txt` (optional)

If you'd like to visualize how the transport network looks like, you can use a few convinient functions from [{gtfstools}](https://github.com/ipea/gtfstools/), our sister package.

```{r poa_small_shapes_sf, message = FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(gtfstools)

# get spatial geometries of GTFS
shapes_sf <- gtfstools::get_shapes_geometry(poa)
stops_sf <- gtfstools::get_stops_geometry(poa)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = shapes_sf) +
  geom_sf(data = stops_sf, color = "red", size = .2)
```

Some times, GTFS feeds come with internal inconsistencies, for example with trips going too fast, or not accounting for dwell time, etc. We highly recommend that you use {gtfstools} functions to profile, clean and edit your GTFS data before running {gtfs2gps} on it. In this example below, we run `gtfstools::fix_gtfs()` a simple and convinient function to fix a few of these issues. Here, we use this function to cap max speed to 25 Km/h and set a min dwell time of 30 secs, and the funcion recalculates the stop times of the feed.

```{r poa_small_shapes_sf, message = FALSE}
# quick fix
poa_fixed <- gtfstools::fix_gtfs(
  gtfs = poa, 
  max_speed = 25, 
  min_dwell_time = 30
  )

```


# Converting to GPS-like format

To convert GTFS to GPS-like format, use `gtfs2gps()`. This is the core function of the package. It takes a GTFS zipped file as an input and returns a `data.table` where each row represents a 'GPS-like' data point for every trip in the GTFS file. In summary, this function interpolates the space-time position of each vehicle in each trip considering the network distance and average speed between stops. The function samples the timestamp of each vehicle every $100m$ by default, but the user can set a different value in the `spatial_resolution` argument. See the example below.

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
poa_gps <- gtfs2gps(
  gtfs_data = poa_fixed, 
  spatial_resolution = 100, 
  ncores = 1
  )

```

obs. Remember you can user the argument `ncores` to set how many 
threads the function can use to parallelize operations. Setting
`ncores` to `4` or `6` can lead to substantial reductions in 
computation time in large GTFS feeds.



# Visualizing gtfs2gps output

The output of the `gtfs2gps()` looks like this. Like a traditional 
table of a GPS data set, with each row marking the timestamp and 
location of each vechile of every trip schedulded in the GTFS.

```{r, message = FALSE}

head(poa_gps)

```
 The following figure maps the first 100 data points of the sample data we processed. They can be converted to `simple feature` points or linestring.

```{r, message = FALSE}
poa_gps60 <- poa_gps[1:100, ]

# points
poa_gps60_sfpoints <- gps_as_sfpoints(poa_gps60)

# linestring
poa_gps60_sflinestring <- gps_as_sflinestring(poa_gps60)

# plot
plot(sf::st_geometry(poa_gps60_sfpoints), pch = 20)
plot(sf::st_geometry(poa_gps60_sflinestring), col = "blue", add = TRUE)
box()
```

The function `gtfs2gps()` automatically recognizes whether the GTFS data brings detailed `stop_times.txt` information or whether it is a `frequencies.txt` GTFS file. A sample data of a GTFS with detailed  `stop_times.txt` can be found below:

```{r, message = FALSE}
poa <- system.file("extdata/poa.zip", package ="gtfs2gps")

poa_gps <- gtfs2gps(poa, spatial_resolution = 50)

poa_gps_sfpoints <- gps_as_sfpoints(poa_gps)

plot(sf::st_geometry(poa_gps_sfpoints[1:200,]))

box()
```

# Methodological note

For a given trip, the function `gtfs2gps` calculates the average speed between each pair of consecutive stops given by the ratio between cumulative network distance `S` and departure time `t` for a consecutive pair of valid stop_ids (`i`), 

```{r equation, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("https://github.com/ipea/gtfs2gps/blob/master/man/figures/equation1.png?raw=true")
```

Since the beginning of each trip usually starts before the first stop_id, the mean speed cannot be calculated as shown in the previous equation because information on `i` period does not exist. In this case, the function consider the mean speed for the whole trip. It also happens after the last valid stop_id (`N`) of the trips, where info on `i + 1` also does not exist. 

```{r speed, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("https://github.com/ipea/gtfs2gps/blob/master/man/figures/speed.PNG?raw=true")
```
